title: Who should deliver employment support?
label: 18 November 2026 · Local employment support
summary: The committee explored why employment support in the UK is centrally run, what local control could improve, and the risks of shifting responsibility to regional bodies. The witnesses supported giving local areas more room to shape services around people and employers, but stressed that devolution needs stable funding, skilled staff, reliable data, clear accountability and regular evaluation. Central Government should still set some standards and step in when services fail or particular groups are overlooked.

speakers.label: Professor Dan Finn
speakers.name: Professor Dan Finn
speakers.role: Emeritus Professor of Social Inclusion, University of Portsmouth

glossary.definition: The national network of offices that helps people find work and administers working-age benefits.
The Department for Work and Pensions, which runs benefits and much of the UK's employment support.
Rules requiring some people receiving benefits to take agreed steps towards finding or preparing for work.
Reductions or suspensions of benefits that can follow when someone doesn't meet certain requirements.
A programme offering employment support, including help for people facing health-related barriers to work.
A programme providing employment support to people who have been unemployed for a long time.
Regional bodies, often led by elected mayors, that coordinate services and may take on powers from central government.
A young person who isn't in education, employment or training.
An organisation that gathers and tests evidence to help public services understand which approaches work.

chapters.title: Why the system is run from the centre
chapters.takeaway: The national system grew around benefit rules and central targets, which makes it easier for government to act consistently but harder to tailor help to local needs.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Why has employment support in the UK become so centralised, and what are the advantages and drawbacks?

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: The system changed over time. It began as a public employment service focused on the wider jobs market, skills and matching people to vacancies. As unemployment rose, government increasingly focused it on people claiming unemployment benefits.

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: That made the service useful to central government: it could encourage people to look for work, help control benefit spending and respond quickly to economic shocks. But it also meant that Jobcentre Plus became more focused on benefit claimants than on everyone who might need help finding work.

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: Some people receiving benefits must meet work-related requirements, known as conditionality, and can face sanctions if they don't. That remains a major part of the jobcentre's work. Central government has also tended to favour uniform national programmes rather than let areas decide how to deliver them.

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: The UK state is highly centralised, and the DWP has a large role in running benefits and a national network of jobcentres. That encourages the department to manage services centrally.

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: There's also a cycle: government says local areas don't yet have the skills to take on responsibility, but they may only build those skills by taking on some responsibility. Past programmes that appeared to work have also encouraged government to repeat similar national models.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Can national standards still protect quality while local areas have more freedom?

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: Yes, but we don't yet know the right balance. Government can set minimum expectations while allowing local services to work with nearby health and other services. Programmes such as Connect to Work and WorkWell are being combined more flexibly in some places; we should learn from how that goes.

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: A major risk of devolution is that local areas might be rewarded for moving people off one benefit, even if they don't find lasting work and end up needing support elsewhere. Costs can simply shift to another part of government.

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: There are other risks too: people may lose contact with support, or local programmes may be pleasant but fail to help people into jobs. Weak checks on providers could also mean poor use of public money. Government needs to keep track of whether employment is actually improving.

chapters.title: Lessons from other countries
chapters.takeaway: Other countries show that local delivery can work, but only with careful planning, clear responsibilities and support to build local skills.

turns.speaker: John Milne
turns.text: What does international experience tell us about local and national models?

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: Many countries have moved towards local delivery, though their systems and constitutions differ from ours. Canada, for example, transferred staff, budgets and computer systems to provincial and local services. That took time and required changes in how people worked.

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: Local delivery can bring employment, health and other services together in ways a national service may struggle to do. But it needs careful design, especially so that local authorities are encouraged to help people into lasting work rather than simply reduce benefit claims.

turns.speaker: John Milne
turns.text: Are there clear lessons about how to manage the change?

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: Yes. In Canada, local areas were expected to assess their own programmes. Places that needed help developed evaluation plans with the national government, building the ability to judge results for themselves over time.

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: Denmark shows the value of making it clear who is responsible for what, and giving people a clear place to go for support. Our system is less tidy: some services are local while jobcentres still handle other parts.

turns.speaker: John Milne
turns.text: What is the Government proposing for England?

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: The plans set out local employment support through strategic authorities, with funding going to some authorities through combined budgets. The Government has also said it wants strategic authorities across England by 2028, but there are still important details to settle.

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: For example, it's not yet clear how employment support will be devolved in places without a mayor, how local leaders will be held to account, or what support there will be for people unemployed for a long time as Restart ends. There are also questions about whether the proposed transfer of some education funding for 16-to-19-year-olds covers all or only part of that budget.

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: When money is devolved without being reserved for a specific service, it can become hard to see where it went. In Scotland and Northern Ireland, for example, funding linked to Restart wasn't tied to a dedicated programme for long-term unemployed people. We need to be able to track both the money and the results.

chapters.title: Skills, budgets and local capacity
chapters.takeaway: Local areas need more expertise and reliable funding to take on new duties, but they must be allowed to build that capacity as responsibilities shift.

turns.speaker: Liz Twist
turns.text: Strategic authorities are taking on duties in employment, housing and transport. Do they have enough capacity to do all of this?

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: It will vary a lot. Places with more experience have often had time to build skills gradually; the next expansion is expected to happen faster. We see three important gaps: designing policy, analysing local needs and results, and buying services well.

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: Local teams need information about who lives in their area, what jobs are available and whether their programmes work. They also need to negotiate contracts with large providers, small businesses and charities, and make sure those services offer good value.

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: Some places have had a smoother start with Connect to Work than others. That may reflect both the experience of the authority and whether people in different organisations already know how to work together. The answer can't be to wait for every area to be fully ready, or local capacity may never grow.

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: Central government should help build local expertise, including sharing its experience buying and managing services. Local authorities already have relevant skills, but there will be uneven performance during the transition.

turns.speaker: Liz Twist
turns.text: What would help local areas manage that transition?

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: They need access to data so they can identify who needs help, judge whether support works and check the performance of organisations delivering it. Sharing information across services remains a major difficulty.

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: Staff could also spend time working between central government and local authorities, sharing experience. But national officials shouldn't assume they have all the answers; local areas already have valuable knowledge.

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: Jobcentre Plus has regional and local management teams too, so staff could share knowledge in both directions rather than treating everything as a choice between Westminster and local government.

turns.speaker: Liz Twist
turns.text: Local government budgets are already under pressure. Will the money follow these new responsibilities?

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: That's a key risk. If money is tightly reserved, local authorities may just deliver a national programme in a different way. If they have more freedom, government needs another way to make sure people receive support.

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: One possible approach is for local authorities to keep some savings if they help people into work sooner, and reinvest the money in services. But Finland found that making local authorities responsible for the cost of benefits can leave some with large bills and less money to provide support.

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: There is also a risk of imposing legal duties or guarantees without funding them. Minimum standards matter, but very detailed requirements can push services to meet the rules rather than achieve better results.

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: Local government already has expensive legal duties in areas such as social care and housing. Adding another duty without enough money could crowd out other services. Funding and responsibilities need to be agreed together.

chapters.title: Bringing services and employers together
chapters.takeaway: Local partnerships can tackle the problems behind unemployment, but they need practical ways to cooperate and employers need a clear point of contact.

turns.speaker: Liz Twist
turns.text: What can other countries teach us about making services work together?

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: In the United States, American Job Centers bring many services together in one place. Typically, around 18 organisations coordinate their work, with some responsible for funding and running the centre.

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: Setting up this kind of service usually takes three to five years. Staff, computer systems and data-sharing arrangements all have to change, and the system needs continued adjustment afterwards.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What has worked in previous efforts to localise support?

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: Earlier programmes were often tightly controlled from the centre. As unemployment fell, local teams found that a standard programme didn't always fit the needs of the people they served. Local partnerships helped develop skills and experience that some regional authorities still draw on.

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: Evidence-based programmes can become too rigid if staff are judged mainly on whether they followed the process. We need to see whether people get and keep jobs, and to evaluate what local teams change so others can learn from it.

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: Local areas should be able to try a different approach when they have a good reason to think it will work better. They should monitor results, investigate when things go wrong and be prepared for central government to help turn around poor performance.

turns.speaker: Andrew Pakes
turns.text: People out of work may also need help with health, housing, skills or poverty. How can local services work around those overlapping needs?

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: Local services can be better placed to respond because people use health and other support locally. Flexible, lasting funding and the ability to share budgets can help organisations work together. Simply ordering them to cooperate doesn't guarantee better results.

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: It helps to have a couple of organisations clearly responsible for steering the work, with other services agreeing how they will contribute. In one example from Manchester, local teams found that poor dental health was a barrier to getting work, so they arranged support with university dental trainees.

turns.speaker: Andrew Pakes
turns.text: What role can employers play?

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: Regional authorities may be able to work with large employers at a useful scale, while also involving smaller businesses. Employers need a clear place to go when they have vacancies; the current mix of different programmes can be confusing.

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: Employers can help shape training for real vacancies and identify routes into skilled jobs, rather than just immediate entry-level work. A coordinated service can also stop several small providers competing for the same employers and job openings.

turns.speaker: Andrew Pakes
turns.text: Some regions are newer and cover several different local job markets. How can they build the organisations and relationships needed to deliver?

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: Stable, long-term funding makes it easier to hire staff, develop services and become a reliable partner for employers. Areas with several centres may need to build skills across a wider geography than a single-city region.

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: Frequent reorganisations make this harder. Staff may not know what their jobs or responsibilities will be in six months, and areas without a history of working together may struggle to agree on priorities.

turns.speaker: Andrew Pakes
turns.text: Should highly specialised support stay national, for example for deaf or blind people?

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: It depends on the group and the scale needed. A regional authority may have enough people to organise many specialist services, but some very small groups may need a national programme.

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: Devolution doesn't stop central government from intervening if a group isn't getting suitable help. Canada, for instance, has some national services for specific communities, delivered directly or through local and voluntary organisations.

chapters.title: Accountability and learning what works
chapters.takeaway: Local freedom needs public information about results and people's experiences, as well as a way to intervene when support falls short.

turns.speaker: Steve Darling
turns.text: Is the country ready for this major change, or could expectations run ahead of what local organisations can deliver?

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: I'm encouraged by the growing links between employment and health services, such as putting employment advisers in health settings. But the ambition may be greater than the capacity available. If people expect too much too quickly, they may decide the whole approach has failed.

turns.speaker: Steve Darling
turns.text: Will local leaders have real freedom, or will central rules still control what they do?

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: Some current agreements still emphasise activity counts, such as how many people start a programme, rather than whether they find lasting work. That could change, but we need to see how the new arrangements work.

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: A local accounting officer should be answerable for local spending and results, but we need clarity on how that responsibility connects to Parliament and local scrutiny. Public information and local media attention also matter.

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: My hope is that devolution makes a confusing patchwork of services more coherent. My concern is that different areas might try different approaches without properly evaluating them or sharing what they learn.

turns.speaker: Steve Darling
turns.text: Could the Local Government Association help local areas share good practice?

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: It could be part of the answer, alongside the DWP and evidence organisations. We don't necessarily need a new organisation, but we do need a reliable way to share learning beyond informal personal contacts.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What should national and local performance measures look at?

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: They should measure results such as getting a job, staying in work and increasing earnings, but also people's experience of the support. Surveys can reveal whether people got the help they were promised, and sometimes uncover jobs that official records missed.

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: We publish some information about Restart providers, but we don't have the same clear public picture of people's experiences in jobcentres. Evaluations often arrive too late to fix problems while a programme is still running.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So should people using services help shape them too?

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: Yes. Australia has used people's feedback as part of its system for assessing providers. We should also evaluate early, so we can see what is going wrong and make changes, while still checking longer-term results later.

turns.speaker: Neil Duncan-Jordan
turns.text: Can other countries show us how to measure success more reliably?

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: In the United States, earnings records can show whether people's pay improves after they enter work. Linking tax and employment information could help us measure not just job starts but whether people's earnings rise.

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: But not everyone without work claims benefits, so benefit records can't tell us what happens to them. Representative surveys can help, without asking every provider to chase each person's proof of employment.

turns.speaker: Neil Duncan-Jordan
turns.text: Does evidence by itself decide which employment policies a country chooses?

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: No. Evidence informs political choices but doesn't settle them. In the United States, for example, there has been more attention to training for career paths, not only getting someone into any available job.

turns.speaker: Neil Duncan-Jordan
turns.text: Are local areas collecting enough reliable evidence now?

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: Often not. Some claims that a programme works rely heavily on what providers report, without enough independent checking. A What Works Centre could help, but its findings need to arrive quickly enough to guide decisions.

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: We also need to study who takes part. People who choose to join employment programmes may not represent everyone who is out of work because of ill health. Local support might reach people who are reluctant to approach a national department, but we need to test that rather than assume it.

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: Health services could also ask about people's work and record how they help people stay in jobs. A lot of that support isn't currently captured in employment data.

turns.speaker: Neil Duncan-Jordan
turns.text: What does Denmark's experience suggest about reducing rules and relying on results?

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: Denmark devolved employment services to local government, then reduced detailed rules and cut the budget, expecting payment based on results to be enough. But some people stopped being seen. It's a warning that cutting procedures can also mean losing contact with people who need help.

turns.speaker: Professor Dan Finn
turns.text: Accountability shouldn't rely only on financial penalties. Taking money from a struggling area may make it harder to improve. Public comparisons between similar places, backed by reliable data, and the ability for central government to step in may work better.

turns.speaker: Ben Paxton
turns.text: Local scrutiny committees and elected leaders need the information and resources to challenge how services are doing. Parliament should also be able to assess results across areas.
